subject: Computer Networking
title: TLS for Email
description: A fast breakdown of TLS for Email for builders.

hook.text: Emails sent without encryption are readable by any server in the path. TLS fixes that.

buildup.text: STARTTLS upgrades an SMTP connection to encrypted. The mail flies in a TLS tunnel between servers.

discovery.text: MTA-STS forces TLS. Without it, a server can downgrade to plaintext and you'd never know.

twist.text: TLS encrypts the link, not the message. Each server decrypts, reads, then re-encrypts for the next hop.

climax.text: Google's transparency report shows 90%+ of Gmail traffic now uses TLS in transit. Huge progress.

punchline.text: TLS protects email in transit. Not perfect, but essential.

quiz.question: What does STARTTLS do for an SMTP connection?
options: Upgrades it from plaintext to encrypted TLS
Compresses the email to reduce size
Adds a digital signature to the message

details.summary: TLS encrypts email in transit between servers using STARTTLS, which upgrades a plain SMTP connection to encrypted. Without TLS, email travels as readable plain text across the internet. Most major email providers now encrypt server-to-server connections, but enforcement is not universal.
details.whyItMatters: Without TLS, every email you send can be read by anyone who intercepts the network traffic. TLS encryption protects email content during transmission between servers.
takeaways: STARTTLS upgrades plain SMTP to encrypted connections
Without TLS, email is readable plain text on the network
Most major providers encrypt server-to-server email by default

faq.question: Is TLS the same as end-to-end email encryption?
faq.answer: No. TLS encrypts email between servers during transit, but each server decrypts it. The email is readable at each relay point. End-to-end encryption like PGP encrypts the message so only the recipient can read it. TLS protects the pipe; end-to-end encryption protects the message.

faq.question: What happens if the receiving server doesn't support TLS?
faq.answer: Most servers fall back to unencrypted delivery rather than failing. This means a malicious server can strip TLS by pretending not to support it. MTA-STS is a newer standard that tells senders to require TLS and refuse unencrypted delivery for specific domains.
